extracted.intended_audience: The people of the State of New York / informed American citizens and voters
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether and how powers conferred by a proposed federal Constitution are necessary, proper, and limited; and considering the prudence of adopting the Constitution despite procedural irregularities. Targeted commentary addressed to citizens deciding on ratification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of the convention vs. merit of the advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the convention exceeded its formal commission, its proposals are merely advisory and 'to be submitted to the people themselves'; the question for acceptance is not so much from whom the advice comes as whether the advice be good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Constitution 'is to be of no more consequence than the paper on which it is written, unless it be stamped with the approbation of those to whom it is addressed.' Therefore, a recommendation that advances the people's happiness may be embraced despite irregularity of authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of conferred powers for the public good
rubrics_metrics.description: Before conferring any power on the general government, decide whether such a power is necessary to attain a necessary end for the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that political institutions require choosing the greater, not the perfect, good; where a power is necessary, accept it but 'guard as effectually as possible against a perversion of the power to the public detriment.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Guarding against perversion of delegated power
rubrics_metrics.description: When granting powers, accompany them with as many safeguards as possible to prevent their perversion to private or oppressive ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even necessary powers must be accompanied by institutional checks; the Constitution should be read and structured to minimize opportunities for usurpation or abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify governmental powers by their objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers conferred on the federal government should be reviewed in categories related to: (1) security against foreign danger; (2) regulation of intercourse with foreign nations; (3) maintenance of harmony among the States; (4) miscellaneous objects of general utility; (5) restraint of States from injurious acts; and (6) provisions to give efficacy to these powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyzing powers by these classes helps determine both necessity and appropriate limits for each functional area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers for security against foreign danger
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes powers to declare war, grant letters of marque, provide armies and fleets, regulate and call forth the militia, and levy and borrow money — all necessary for national self-defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Security is a primitive object of society; means of security must be commensurate with danger. Limiting defensive resources (e.g., forbidding peacetime readiness) is impractical unless all other nations are likewise limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to raise and maintain armed forces (including in peace)
rubrics_metrics.description: A federal capacity to raise troops and provide fleets, possibly in peace as well as in war, is involved in the power of self-defense and cannot be safely prohibited by strict constitutional bars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments for limiting such a power must reckon with the inability to limit others' preparations for offense; a union reduces the need for large separate state establishments and thus mitigates the danger of standing forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of appropriations terms for military support
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriations for supporting standing forces should be temporally limited (the Constitution ties such appropriations to two-year terms) to guard against the danger of permanent military establishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare forms of practice (e.g., Britain's de facto annual limitation) fairly; the U.S. structure of frequent elections and a two-year limit on appropriations is a check on usurpation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to provide and maintain a navy
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal power to create and maintain a navy is a clear necessity and is well guarded in the Constitution; maritime strength is essential for defense and commerce protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Union is the source of maritime strength for America; a united country with modest forces is more formidable than disunited states with large standing armies. Naval batteries for repelling foreign enterprises cannot be turned against liberties as some land forces might be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation and calling forth of the militia
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution appropriately vests power in the federal government to regulate and call forth the militia as part of national defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This power is essential and has been 'already sufficiently vindicated and explained' (per the text). It complements other defense powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to levy and borrow money adapted to public needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxation and borrowing powers must be broad enough to supply the means for national defense and public needs, and should not be restricted to external taxation alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revenue from foreign commerce is valuable but variable; a durable system 'meant for duration' must accommodate economic and demographic changes (domestic manufactures, raw-material exports, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of the 'general welfare' clause limited by enumeration
rubrics_metrics.description: The general phrase granting power 'to lay and collect taxes...to provide for the common defense and general welfare' must be read in light of the immediately following enumeration of particular powers; the particulars explain and qualify the general phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject the misconstruction that the general clause alone gives Congress unlimited power to legislate on any subject; the enumerated powers constrain the general language and prevent absurd overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal control over foreign relations (treaties, ambassadors, consuls)
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers to make treaties and to send and receive ambassadors, ministers, and consuls properly belong to the federal government and are improvements on the Confederation (which lacked clarity and scope).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including 'other public ministers and consuls' remedies gaps in the Confederation (e.g., ambassadors alone exclude inferior grades and consuls); minute provisions lessen pretexts for gradual usurpation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal power to define and punish piracy and high-seas felonies
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary for the federal government to define and punish piracies, felonies on the high seas, and offenses against the law of nations to ensure uniformity and to prevent individual states embroiling the Confederacy with foreign powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common law or statute definitions from other nations are unsuitable as defaults; for certainty and uniformity, legislative definition by the federal government is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation of foreign commerce and the slave importation clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation of foreign commerce is properly a federal power; the clause postponing power to prohibit the importation of slaves until 1808 is a pragmatic concession viewed as 'a great point gained in favor of humanity' because it provides a path to eventual abolition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although immediate prohibition would be preferable, the twenty-year postponement was a realistic compromise likely to encourage eventual abolition by federal and state action.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to prioritize substance over formal procedure in major constitutional changes
rubrics_metrics.description: In great changes of established governments, forms ought to give way to substance; informal or unauthorized propositions by patriotic citizens may be essential to propose plans that the people can approve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (committees, congresses, state conventions) show that necessary constitutional innovations often arose from irregular but salutary exercises of initiative; the people's approbation ultimately remedies antecedent irregularities.
